sites.name: Sulphide Glacier camp
sites.capacity: A broad flat plateau on the ridgeline with room for several parties, though the daily permit quota caps how many can legitimately be there
sites.water: Usually available — running water is often audible and reachable over the rocks near camp — but this is a snowmelt supply that varies with the year and the week. Bring the means to melt snow and treat found water as likely rather than certain.
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry (wilderness) permit required — this is a DIFFERENT authority from the Mt Baker side, and a Forest Service pass does not cover it. Permits come through Recreation.gov, with a spring early-access lottery followed by a general on-sale, and a share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Reservation and per-person nightly fees apply — these permits are no longer free. The zone carries a small daily party quota.
sites.notes: The standard high camp for the most straightforward route on Shuksan and the best launching point for the summit pyramid. The plateau is flat, spacious and well positioned, and a privy has been maintained on the ridgeline here in recent seasons, which is unusual at this elevation. The permit is the binding constraint on the whole trip rather than the terrain, so plan the paperwork before the climb. Snow covers the site into early summer, and late in the season the approach turns to loose ground and heather that is harder work than the mileage suggests.

sites.name: Shannon Ridge crest camps, below the park boundary
sites.capacity: A few small sites along the open ridge; adequate but cramped compared to the Sulphide camp above
sites.water: Poor. There is essentially nothing between the trailhead streams and the Sulphide Glacier itself, and what does exist on the ridge is gone by late June in most years. Carry water up from the bottom.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE the national park boundary — no backcountry permit needed here, which is the entire reason parties use these sites. A recreation pass is required at the Shannon Ridge trailhead. The park boundary is roughly half a mile further up the ridge, and everything beyond it needs a National Park Service permit.
sites.notes: The fallback for parties who could not get a North Cascades backcountry permit, and honestly worse than the camp above — lower, drier, and leaving a much longer summit day. The trade is administrative rather than scenic, so decide before you drive out whether you would rather chase a walk-up permit at a ranger station. FS Road 1152 and its spur are low elevation and generally open early in the season with no need for high clearance, which makes this the most road-reliable approach to either mountain. Check where the boundary actually falls on your map before pitching a tent, because the ridge does not advertise it clearly.

sites.name: Sulphide Glacier high camp
sites.capacity: Snow platforms only, for one or two parties; no established sites
sites.water: None dependable — melt snow. Anything running at this elevation is a hot-afternoon accident rather than a supply.
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, same as the 6,400 ft camp — through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with fees. Confirm that your permit covers camping this high in the zone rather than assuming.
sites.notes: Some parties carry above the main plateau to shorten summit day to the pyramid, camping on the glacier around 7,500 ft. It is fully exposed, on snow, and above any water, so it only makes sense for a party comfortable with a glacier bivy and a settled forecast. The gain over the lower camp is modest for most people, which is why the 6,400 ft plateau remains the norm. If weather is uncertain, the lower camp is the better place to be.

sites.name: Lake Ann basin
sites.capacity: Established sites around the lake basin; popular with hikers as well as climbers and busy on summer weekends
sites.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams through most of the season. Treat it.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness — the lake sits roughly a mile outside the national park boundary, so no park permit is needed to camp here. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required at the Lake Ann trailhead, camping must be at least two miles from the trailhead between mid-May and mid-November, and the standard 12-person wilderness party limit applies. The permit boundary is signed beyond the lake, and every camp past it needs a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit.
sites.notes: The usual first night for both the Fisher Chimneys and the North Face, and the jurisdictional line running just past it is the single most useful thing to understand about camping on this side of Shuksan — one night at the lake is a Forest Service matter, the next night up on the route is a national park one. The trailhead sits near 4,700 ft and the trail drops before climbing back to the basin, so the return is uphill at the end of a long day. Access is entirely gated by SR 542, plowed to Artist Point on a seasonal schedule and closed with the first serious snowfall in autumn. Snow can linger in the basin into August in a heavy year.

sites.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
sites.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide
sites.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
sites.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.

sites.name: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
sites.capacity: One party; rough ground with a couple of usable spots, not a camp
sites.water: Seasonal melt only. Late in the year expect nothing and carry or melt.
sites.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the approach leaves Forest Service ground shortly past Lake Ann and the bivy is inside the park. Through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; fees apply and the zone quota is small. Do not assume the Lake Ann trailhead pass covers this.
sites.notes: North Face parties share the early approach with the White Salmon Glacier route through a brushy section before the two diverge, and the usual bivy sits near 5,500 ft where the rib abuts the face, above Price Lake. It is a working bivy chosen for position on a serious route rather than for comfort, and the point of it is an early start onto sustained steep snow and ice. Objective hazard governs everything here: the face is avalanche-prone, particularly early in the season and further left, so timing and a cold night matter more than the site itself. This is a spring-into-early-summer route in most years.
